title: Signs of a stroke — note the time and call now
applies_to: Someone whose face has dropped on one side, whose arm has gone weak, or whose speech has suddenly changed.

citations.source: WHO and IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2020
citations.section: Stroke recognition using the FAST check

citations.source: European Resuscitation Council Guidelines 2021: First Aid
World Stroke Organization, Global Stroke Guidelines and Action Plan
citations.section: Public recognition and time to treatment

steps.text: Ask them to smile. Look for one side of the mouth or face hanging down.
Ask them to lift both arms and hold them up. Look for one arm drifting back down.
Ask them to say a simple sentence after you. Listen for slurred or muddled words.
If even one of those three looks wrong, call for an ambulance now and say you think it is a stroke.
Look at a clock. Note the time the signs started, or the last time they were their normal self.
Help them sit or lie down with the head and shoulders raised a little. If they are being sick, roll them onto their side.
Loosen tight clothing. Keep the room quiet and keep them warm.
Stay with them and keep watching. The signs can get worse quickly.
Say that noted time out loud to the ambulance crew. It decides what treatment the hospital can still give.

do_not: Do not give them anything to eat or drink. Swallowing is often not safe after a stroke.
Do not wait to see whether the signs pass off. The first hours decide how much can be saved.
Do not let them drive, and do not let them go to bed to sleep it off.
Do not let them walk about if one side is weak. They will fall.
Do not give them anything to take for it. Only a hospital can tell which kind of stroke this is.
escalate_if: They stop answering you and stop breathing normally — start pushing on the chest.
They are being sick, have the worst headache of their life, or start shaking — say this on the phone.
The signs go away on their own — they still need to be seen today. That can be a warning of a bigger one.
They are already being treated for a heart or blood problem — tell the crew that.
They have been out in strong heat and are hot to touch — start cooling them while you wait. Being overcome by heat can look like this.
